claims.text: FCC metals with low stacking-fault energy exhibit higher ductility.
Copper is an FCC metal with low stacking-fault energy.
The higher ductility of low-stacking-fault-energy FCC metals arises from easy dislocation glide and cross-slip.
Introducing nanoscale twins through severe plastic deformation enhances ductility.
The initial material is polycrystalline copper with an average grain size of 10 micrometers.
Copper is to be processed by ECAP at a strain rate of 0.1 s^-1 and a temperature of 293 K.
ECAP will increase twin density by 20%.
ECAP will decrease dislocation density by 15%.
Copper has a stacking-fault energy of 40 mJ/m² under the stated conditions.
Low stacking-fault energy facilitates dislocation glide and cross-slip in copper.
Nanoscale twins reduce the critical stress for dislocation glide and cross-slip by 10%.
ECAP processing will increase elongation at break by 45–50% relative to baseline.
ECAP-processed copper will have an absolute elongation at break of 50–55%.
As-received polycrystalline copper has 40% elongation at break.
A ductility increase of at least 10% represents a practical improvement in formability and resistance to cracking.
Microstructural and defect variations may affect the measured ductility outcome.
The proposed roles of nanoscale twins and dislocation density may not fully capture the underlying deformation mechanisms.

contradictions.description: A 45–50% relative increase from a 40% elongation baseline implies an absolute elongation of 58–60%, not the stated 50–55%. Conversely, 50–55% absolute elongation corresponds to a relative increase of 25–37.5%.
